ety.text: From Middle English an, from Old English ān (“a, an”, literally “one”). More at one.
From Middle English an (“and, if”). Doublet of and.
From the Old English an, on (preposition).

ex: I'll be there in half an hour.
'E's staying at an 'otel. (compare He's staying at a hotel.)

senses.d: Used before /h/ in a stressed or unstressed syllable.
ex: This is an historic honor which matches the weight of our times.

senses.d: Used before one and words with initial ⟨u⟩, ⟨eu⟩ when pronounced /ju/.

ex: […] An the worst fall that ever fell, I hope I shall make shift to go without him.
An it harm none, do what ye will.

At length did cross an Albatross,
 Thorough the Fog it came;
 And an it were a Christian Soul,
 We hail'd it in God's Name.

senses.d: The first letter of the Georgian alphabet, ა (Mkhedruli), Ⴀ (Asomtavruli) or ⴀ (Nuskhuri).
In each; to or for each; per.
ex: I was only going twenty miles an hour.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French un, from Old French un, from Latin ūnum, accusative singular of ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Old French une, from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus.
Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Old Spanish un, from uno, from Latin ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”).

es:una.gl: one (an indefinite plural pronoun using a singular feminine item, used for females)

ety.text: Inherited from Old Spanish una (“an; a”), from Latin ūna, feminine of ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one, single”).
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese ũu (“one; a”), from Latin ūnum (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos (“one”). Doublet of uno.
From Latin sī (“if”) or from Late Latin se(d), from Latin sī and quid ("what").
